title: When Sleep Problems Need Help
hook: Better sleep habits fix a lot — but not everything. Loud snoring with gasping, or weeks of being unable to sleep, are signals to see a doctor, not push through.
key_points: When good sleep habits aren't enough, a sleep disorder may be the cause.
Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep that lasts and affects your day.
Loud snoring, gasping, and heavy daytime sleepiness can signal sleep apnea.
Persistent sleep problems are worth raising with a doctor — they're treatable.
content_html: Good sleep hygiene — a dark room, a steady schedule, easing off screens and caffeine — solves most ordinary sleep trouble. But when you've done all that and still can't sleep, or you're sleeping through the night and still exhausted, the problem may be a genuine sleep disorder, and pushing through isn't the answer.
extra_html: The NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute describes how ongoing poor sleep can signal an underlying condition. Insomnia — persistent trouble falling or staying asleep that drags on your days — is one. Sleep apnea is another, and its tell-tale signs are worth knowing: loud snoring, gasping or pauses in breathing during sleep (often noticed by a partner), and heavy daytime sleepiness despite enough hours in bed. The encouraging part is that these are recognized, treatable conditions. If sleep problems persist despite solid habits, or those apnea signs sound familiar, raise it with a doctor. This is general guidance, not a substitute for medical advice.

source.name: NIH National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

related.title: Why Sleep Matters
related.hook: Sleep isn't downtime — it's when your brain consolidates memory and your body repairs itself. Skimp on it for long and the bill comes due in your health.

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

related.title: When a Symptom Needs a Doctor
related.hook: Most everyday symptoms pass on their own. The skill worth having is recognizing the red flags that mean don't wait — call for help now.

flashcards.prompt: What are warning signs that snoring might be sleep apnea?
flashcards.back_html: Loud snoring paired with gasping or pauses in breathing during sleep, plus heavy daytime sleepiness. These are reasons to see a doctor — sleep apnea is treatable.

flashcards.prompt: When should ordinary sleep tips give way to seeing a doctor?

choices.text: When sleep problems persist and disrupt your daily life despite good habits
Only after a single bad night's sleep
Never — sleep disorders always fix themselves

flashcards.explanation_html: The NIH NHLBI notes that persistent sleep problems despite good habits may be a sleep disorder worth raising with a doctor, since many are treatable.
